text: A young wife, out of food, collapses at the door of an outlaw, who takes one look and decides she is his. His companion, Widow Ma, was there first and has no plan to move. Yim Ho gives this three-cornered household 104 minutes, which is brief for a story about who owns whom and long enough for the terms to set hard. The pull of it is not romance but arithmetic: one man holds the food, two women live on his decisions, and being chosen and being taken are named by the same word. Made in Hong Kong in 1996 and spoken in Mandarin, it looks at a countryside where a woman's position is settled by men who have already agreed among themselves. What it watches most closely is not what Pan Hao wants. It is the small room the two women are left, and what they do inside it.

A death in the family brings David back to Buenos Aires, and a second one is already on his mother's calendar. He is young, heavy, gay, afraid of flying, and handled by his relatives as a son rather than as a man with a life of his own. Iair Said keeps the film to seventy-five minutes, too short for the long arc of mourning, which leaves the awkward middle of it: relatives, meals, paperwork, the distance between an event and the arrangements people make around it. Nothing here is decided by David. That is the pressure of the thing, a man who has organized his existence around avoidance, kept in rooms where the largest decision of the family's year proceeds without needing his consent, in a city he left and now has to be a son in again.

The other party in this film is an owl, kept in the filmmaker's house for fourteen years, and the length of that number is most of the argument. Seventeen minutes, Japan, 1999, made as a semi-documentary about a bond neither species has a word for. The narration is held down almost to nothing and the images are kept clean, which leaves the strangeness of the attachment nowhere to hide and no tone of voice to soften it. Films about animals generally explain: habitat, behaviour, the useful facts. This one watches instead, and admits early that mortality is part of any arrangement that lasts fourteen years. What it arrives at is closer to intimacy than to natural history, and it does not apologize for the difference.

Two strangers carry an injured man into a Kathmandu hospital, hand him over to his relatives, and part. She is twenty-six, back from years of trying to write poetry in the city and leaving for her village at dawn. He is thirty-three, a guide from India, also going in the morning. Chance returns them to each other with nowhere to sleep and a handful of hours to spend, and the streets and alleys take over the work a plot would otherwise do. Mohan Rai builds on the oldest structure available, two people walking until it gets light, and stakes the film on a proposition that is hard to fake: that a person can be different by morning without a single thing occurring that would look like an event from outside.

A twenty-year-old delinquent is sent to a small-town sawmill, and within a day of arriving he is wearing the collar and running the parish. He is devout, which is the complication. The town has a death from the previous year to get through, and it takes to him. Jan Komasa spends 116 minutes on whether a fraud can do the work, the visits and the confessions and the burials, the daily obligation to say something usable to people in pain, and the film treats neither the belief nor the deception as a joke. Poland gave it the national award for best film. Every act of grace the young man performs is also evidence against him, which keeps the ordinary business of a parish under a pressure it does not usually carry.

Something goes under the wheels of Vero's car, and she does not stop to find out what. What follows is not an investigation. Lucrecia Martel stays with the state the collision leaves her in rather than with the facts of it: relatives being kind, a household able to make an inconvenience disappear for one of its own, days closing over a question nobody wants asked. Eighty-seven minutes, and the suspense is social. In this part of Argentina certain kinds of trouble generate paperwork and certain kinds do not, and the film knows precisely which family it is standing inside. Argentine critics keep it near the top of their own surveys and it turns up abroad on lists of the century's films; neither fact prepares a newcomer for how quietly it works.

The hero runs a projector for a living, which turns out to be less a job than a method. It is 1924, and the plot is no larger than a stolen pocket watch and the rival who arranged the theft: the projectionist wants to be a detective, and the case that finally arrives is his own. The film is built on the idea that a screen is somewhere a person can fall into, and that the fall has consequences a body then has to absorb. Its gags are engineering, all distance and timing and an object arriving exactly where it must, so the laugh comes from accuracy rather than from anyone selling it. Buster Keaton directs. At forty-five minutes there is no room to pad, and the whole of it goes to things that had to be worked out on paper first.

The boy keeps a running comparison between his own troubles and the worse luck of people he has heard about, and for a while it holds. Sweden, 1959: he is sent off to an aunt and uncle while adults deal with what they will not explain to him, and the new place turns out to have its own supply of people managing badly and getting by anyway. Lasse Hallström keeps the camera at a child's eye level and lets the episodes stand without drawing morals out of them, which is why the funny parts and the bleak parts are so often the same parts. Sweden's own best-film award went to it. What stays afterward is the method rather than the story: comparison as a form of comfort, and the strain of keeping it going.

A woman comes home in the afternoon, falls asleep, and the fourteen minutes that follow decline to agree with one another. A path, a figure ahead of her, a house entered again and again, every pass through the same few objects arriving slightly out of true. Maya Deren treats a dream as an editing problem: time and space set deliberately out of register with the objective account of them, so that images legible one at a time turn unaccountable in sequence. The dread is manufactured by arrangement, not by anything announced as a threat. Both the critics' and the directors' Sight and Sound polls have carried it, rare company for a film of a quarter of an hour, and the reason shows early, in how much unease a staircase can be made to hold.

The only thing that can stop a girl, a scarecrow, a tin man and a lion is a witch with a grievance. Everything else in Oz is negotiable: the road is long, the companions agree to come, and the requests are modest, a brain and a heart and some courage, put one at a time to a wizard who receives petitions. The Academy's prize for color photography went to this, and it was the right prize, because the color is structural rather than decorative, telling anyone watching which world they are standing in and what sort of trouble it holds. A hundred and two minutes, on a shape a child can keep in mind, leave and meet and walk and ask. Very little in it is accidental, which is unusual for a film assembled to please everybody at once.

The man who starts all of this is a filmmaker, and the expedition is a shoot. Carl Denham wants footage nobody else has, which is how his leading lady Ann Darrow and his first mate Jack Driscoll come to be standing on an island where a local legend proves to be neither beast nor man. The 1933 picture is unusually clear about its own trade: the creature is taken alive in order to be billed, exhibited and sold tickets to, and the men arranging that are in the same line of work as the men who made the film. A hundred minutes, and the middle of it is spectacle built by hand at a point when the tools for such a thing barely existed. The fear in it is not only about size. It is about how fast a wonder becomes an attraction.

A famous physicist is only half the subject here; the other half is the Cambridge student who falls in love with him. Stephen Hawking is the occasion for the film and Jane Wilde is its second center, and the Academy's recognition of both leads is a fair reading of where the weight sits. A hundred and twenty-three minutes, English, carefully appointed, and the time goes not to cosmology but to the upkeep of two lives fastened to each other: who is owed what, who adjusts, who says the encouraging thing again. The physics stays at a level a dinner guest could follow, a decision rather than a shortfall. James Marsh is filming the years around the work instead of the work, and the interest lies in how much room one household turns out to have.

The acting prize went to the woman who helps, not to the young man whose life it is. Michael Oher is homeless and carrying more than a mainstream picture is willing to sit inside; he becomes an All-American and a first-round NFL pick, and between those two facts stands a family that took him in. The film's shape is theirs. A hundred and twenty-nine minutes of American studio construction, the discomfort carefully managed, the football filmed for legibility, and it was seen by a great many more people than most Academy contenders reach. The position it offers is worth noticing: rescue, viewed from the side of the rescuer, with gratitude placed where an argument might otherwise go. What it does well and what it declines to do are one decision, made once and kept.

A German teenager in the late 1950s spends a summer with a woman much older than he is, and then she is gone. The rest of Michael Berg's life arranges itself around those months, though it takes him a long while to notice. Years afterward Stephen Daldry puts the two of them in one room again, under conditions that make the earlier intimacy impossible to speak of, and the film becomes something else: an account of what one German generation could and could not ask of the one before it. A hundred and twenty-four minutes, and its hardest material arrives by implication rather than by staging. The Academy's award for actress went to the center of it, a woman the film refuses either to excuse or to explain, and sympathy accumulates anyway.
